t: Maximum Number of Consecutive Values You Can Make: The Reach-Interval Trick
o: We may spend any subset of the coins, a value x is makable if some subset sums to x, and we must return the length of the longest run of consecutive integers starting at 0 that are all makable (0 always is, via the empty subset). Example 1, coins = [1,3]: subsets reach 0, 1, 3, 4 — the run breaks at 2, so the answer is 2. Example 2, coins = [1,1,1,4]: the three 1s cover 0 through 3, then 4 attaches seamlessly to extend coverage to 0 through 7, giving 8. Example 3 reaches 20 with [1,4,10,3,1] once sorted. Constraints allow n up to 4*10^4 and coin values up to 4*10^4, so the total sum approaches 1.6*10^9 — far too large for a subset-sum table over every possible value, which pushes us to reason about whole intervals rather than individual sums.
k: If every value in [0, r] is makable and the next coin v satisfies v <= r + 1, coverage extends to [0, r + v]: v fills the hole at r + 1 and shifts every larger reachable sum along with it.

If the smallest unused coin exceeds r + 1, the value r + 1 is forever unmakeable because all remaining coins are at least that large — so processing coins in sorted order guarantees early termination.
The answer equals reach + 1 because the covered interval [0, reach] includes both endpoints.

a.i: Track every achievable sum in a set seeded with {0}; each coin contributes the shift of the entire current set by its value. Afterward scan upward from 0 until the first gap appears. This mirrors the statement most literally and is easy to verify by hand, but the number of distinct sums can explode toward the total coin value, making it impractical for the largest inputs — it mainly serves as the intuitive stepping stone to the greedy.
s: For each coin v, add s + v to the set for every currently reachable sum s.
Count upward from 0 while consecutive values remain in the set.
Return the count, which includes 0 itself.
a.t: Up to exponential / pseudo-polynomial time — the set can approach the total coin sum (about 1.6*10^9 here), so this degrades badly on adversarial inputs despite being conceptually simple.
a.sp: O(total sum) worst case to hold the reachable set.

a.n: Approach 2: Sort Then Grow the Reach (Greedy)
a.i: Sort coins ascending and maintain reach: the largest R such that every value in [0, R] is makable. The next coin v extends coverage exactly when v <= reach + 1 — it supplies the missing value r + 1 and, combined with the already-guaranteed interval, covers everything up to reach + v. The first coin violating this leaves r + 1 permanently out of reach, since every later coin is even larger, so one pass suffices.
s: Initialize reach = 0 (only the empty sum is guaranteed).
For each coin in order: stop if coin > reach + 1; otherwise set reach += coin.
a.t: O(n log n) — dominated by sorting; the sweep itself is linear.
a.sp: O(1) auxiliary beyond the in-place sort.

w: Present the greedy first in an interview — it is simultaneously the simplest and the optimal solution; mention the subset-sum DP only as the naive baseline you are improving on. Pitfalls: forgetting that the empty subset makes 0 always achievable (the answer is at least 1), using >= instead of > (a coin equal to reach + 1 IS usable), skipping the sort, and overflowing 32-bit accumulators since reach can exceed 10^9. Edge cases worth testing: every coin at least 2 (answer stays 1), and many duplicate 1s. Follow-up: this is the same patching argument behind LC 330 (Patching Array), where coins may also be added to fix gaps.
